title: Using AI Responsibly
hook: The point of AI literacy isn't to use AI for everything — it's to use it well: check its work, be honest that you used it, and know the moments to put it down.
key_points: Verify before you trust — you're responsible for what you pass on as true.
Be transparent when AI did real work, especially at school or at work.
Keep humans in charge of high-stakes calls: health, legal, money, safety.
Use it to assist your thinking, not to replace it.
content_html: Once you understand what AI can and can't do, "responsible use" stops being a vague slogan and becomes a short, practical checklist. It isn't about using AI for everything or avoiding it out of fear — it's about using it well, so it genuinely helps without quietly creating problems. Three habits cover most situations.
extra_html: Verify before you trust. Because AI can be confidently wrong, you're the one accountable for anything you pass on as true — check facts, sources, and numbers before relying on them. Be honest about using it. If AI did real work on something — an essay, a report, an image — transparency matters, and many schools and workplaces now have clear rules; pretending you didn't use it can cross a line. Keep humans on the big decisions. AI can inform a choice about your health, finances, legal situation, or someone's safety, but it shouldn't make that choice. Underneath all three is one idea: AI is a powerful assistant to your judgment, not a replacement for it. Used that way, it makes you faster and better; handed the wheel, it makes mistakes you'll own.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: Bias & Fairness
related.hook: AI learns from data made by people, so it inherits our patterns — including the unfair ones. A model trained on a biased past will confidently recommend a biased future.

related.title: Your Data & Privacy
related.hook: When you type into a free AI tool, you might be the product. What you share can be stored, reviewed by humans, and used to train future models — so share like it's not private.

related.title: How to Fact-Check AI
related.hook: You can't tell a true AI answer from a made-up one by reading it — both sound equally sure. So build a habit: for anything that matters, verify it somewhere that isn't the AI.

related.title: Over-Relying on AI
related.hook: The subtle risk isn't that AI fails — it's that it usually works, so you stop checking. Trusting a confident machine over your own judgment is its own kind of mistake.

flashcards.prompt: Who is responsible for an AI-written answer you share as fact?

choices.text: You are — you should verify it before passing it on
No one, since a machine wrote it

flashcards.explanation_html: AI is a tool you chose to use. Checking its output and standing behind what you share stays your responsibility.

flashcards.prompt: When should a human stay firmly in charge of the decision?
flashcards.back_html: For high-stakes calls — health, legal, financial, or safety — where AI can inform you but shouldn't make the final decision.
